from_notes: Euro-based BS name from 2000 (APPSC 2019); BS-I also called 'India 2000'
x: Euro-based emission norms have been followed in India under the Bharat Stage name since 2000 (BS-I, 'India 2000'). 1991/1992 were the first pre-Euro norms, and 2003 is the National Auto Fuel Policy.
source: Rocket Environment (src/environment/rocket-environment.txt) p.5; app notes 5:100 sub 0

from_notes: BS-VI vehicles manufactured on or after 1 April 2023 must meet OBD Stage II-A requirements
x: OBD is mandatory under BS-VI (OBD Stage II-A from April 2023, II-B from April 2025), so 'OBD not necessary' is the incorrect statement. BS-IV sale ended in 2020, RDE came in for the first time, and BS-IV/BS-VI mirror Euro 4/Euro 6.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.44-45

x: On 29 March 2017 the Supreme Court barred the sale and registration of BS-III (and older) vehicles from 1 April 2017, when BS-IV became nationwide. BS-IV vehicles were barred only from 1 April 2020.
source: cseindia.org (CSE on SC judgement on sale of BS-III vehicles); PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.44
evidence: cseindia.org CSE press release (SC: stop sale of BS-III vehicles from April 1, 2017)

from_notes: BS-VI India from 1 April 2020
x: The Supreme Court barred the sale and registration of BS-IV vehicles from 1 April 2020, the date BS-VI came into force nationwide.
source: Rocket Environment (src/environment/rocket-environment.txt) p.5; Shankar Environment Part 06 (src/environment/shankar-environment-06.ocr.txt) p.13

x: Itai-itai ('ouch-ouch') disease is caused by cadmium, from mining wastewater used to irrigate rice in Japan. Mercury causes Minamata disease.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.12; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.73

from_notes: Itai-itai (ouch-ouch) | Cadmium | Japan; mining wastewater used for irrigation (APPSC 2024)
x: Itai-itai came from cadmium in wastewater from mining upstream that was used to irrigate rice fields in Toyama, Japan, not from seafood, air or pesticides. Seafood (methyl mercury) is the Minamata route.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.73; app notes 5:101 sub 4

from_notes: Nitrate Pollution: Proves lethal for infants, causing blue-baby syndrome or methaemoglobinemia
x: Blue baby syndrome (methaemoglobinaemia) is caused by excess nitrate in drinking water, which forms methaemoglobin that cannot carry oxygen. Fluoride causes fluorosis and arsenic causes arsenicosis.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.12; Shankar Environment Part 06 (src/environment/shankar-environment-06.ocr.txt) p.18

from_notes: Nitrate Pollution: Proves lethal for infants, causing blue-baby syndrome or methaemoglobinemia
x: Blue baby syndrome (methaemoglobinaemia) is caused by excess nitrate in drinking water, which forms methaemoglobin that cannot carry oxygen. Fluoride causes fluorosis and arsenic causes arsenicosis.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.12; Shankar Environment Part 06 (src/environment/shankar-environment-06.ocr.txt) p.18

from_notes: Excess nitrate in drinking water reacts with hemoglobin to form non-functional methaemoglobin
x: The question asks what is present in the blood: excess nitrate forms non-functional methaemoglobin, which is what causes the blueness. Nitrate is the cause in water, not the blood substance.
source: Shankar Environment Part 06 (src/environment/shankar-environment-06.ocr.txt) p.18; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.67

from_notes: Pain in bones and joints, and outward bending of legs from the knees, is called Knock-Knee syndrome.
x: Knock-knee syndrome is a form of skeletal fluorosis from excess fluoride in drinking water (outward bending of the legs from the knees). Mercury, lead and arsenic cause other diseases.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.68

from_notes: Fluoride Contamination: Causes fluorosis, leading to dental problems
x: Dental mottling is a sign of dental fluorosis from excess fluoride in drinking water. Caries and calcification are different conditions.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.12; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.68

from_notes: Fluoride Contamination: Causes fluorosis, leading to dental problems
x: Excess fluoride causes fluorosis, whose dental form shows as mottled teeth. Lung disease and intestinal infection are not the standard answer.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.12; Shankar Environment Part 06 (src/environment/shankar-environment-06.ocr.txt) p.18

from_notes: Fluoride Contamination: Causes fluorosis, leading to dental problems and dysfunctioning of respiratory, neuromuscular, and gastrointestinal systems.
x: Fluoride ion is matched with fluorosis, not indigestion, so pair 4 is the wrong match. Mercury–Minamata, cadmium–Itai-itai and nitrate–blue baby are correct.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.12; Shankar Environment Part 06 (src/environment/shankar-environment-06.ocr.txt) p.18
dispute: Official key / most books: Fluoride – Indigestion is the wrong pair. Strictly: NextGen and Shankar list gastro-intestinal problems among fluorosis effects (NextGen Environment APPSC 10 p.12; Shankar Environment Part 06 p.18), so the pair is not entirely false.

from_notes: Arsenic Poisoning: Leads to black foot disease ... can result in skin and lung cancers.
x: Arsenic in drinking water is a carcinogen: it causes arsenicosis/blackfoot disease and skin and lung cancer. Iron, chlorine and fluorine are not the cancer-causing answer.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.12; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.68

x: Nickel is a common cause of allergic contact dermatitis. Itai-itai is caused by cadmium.
source: general knowledge, not checked (printed key agrees); app notes

x: Minamata (methyl mercury) and Itai-itai (cadmium) are both metal-toxicity diseases, so dermatitis is the exception keyed by SSC.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.12 (Minamata, Itai-itai); general knowledge, not checked (dermatitis)
dispute: Official key / most books: Dermatitis is NOT caused by metal toxicity. Strictly: nickel allergy causes contact dermatitis (keyed so in SSC CGL 2017), so dermatitis can be metal-linked.

from_notes: Mercury Poisoning ... leading to Minamata disease ... Nitrate Pollution ... blue-baby syndrome
x: Mercury (as methyl mercury) causes Minamata disease and nitrate causes blue baby syndrome. Osteoporosis is not the standard mercury or nitrate disease.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.12

from_notes: Seepage of industrial and mine discharges and fly ash ponds of thermal power plants can lead to arsenic in groundwater.
x: Arsenic: agricultural, mining and manufacturing compounds and fly ash; mercury: coal-fired plants, incinerators, gold mining; fluoride: minerals like apatite, micas, hornblende; chromium: tannery wastewater. So option 4 is correct.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.68 (arsenic: fly ash); app notes 5:101

from_notes: High concentrations of DDT disrupt calcium metabolism in birds
x: Mercury causes Minamata, nitrates/phosphates cause eutrophication, high DDT disturbs calcium metabolism in birds (thin eggshells), and cadmium causes Itai-itai.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.73; NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.12

from_notes: The water pollution in river is measured by the dissolved amount of ... Oxygen
x: The level of water pollution in a river is assessed by its dissolved oxygen: more organic pollution means less DO. Chlorine, nitrogen and ozone are not the measure.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.14; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.64

from_notes: [UPSC 2017] Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD) is a standard criterion for
x: BOD is a standard criterion for pollution assay in aquatic ecosystems: it measures the oxygen microbes need to decompose organic matter in water. It has nothing to do with blood, forests or high altitude.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.65 (UPSC 2017 PYQ)

from_notes: [UPSC 2017] Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD) is a standard criterion for

source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.65 (UPSC 2017 PYQ)

from_notes: BOD is the amount of DO needed by aerobic microorganisms to break down biodegradable organic matter present in a water
x: BOD indicates organic pollution in the aquatic environment (water); it is not used for soil or air.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.65

from_notes: A high BOD indicates a high load of organic pollution, meaning microbes consume more oxygen
x: High BOD means a high load of organic matter and microbes consuming oxygen, as with sewage contamination. Low BOD indicates clean water.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.65; NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.14

from_notes: If in any water Body, there is high BOD value then it is generally ... Very polluted
x: High BOD means a high load of organic matter and microbes consuming oxygen, as with sewage contamination. Low BOD indicates clean water.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.65; NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.14

from_notes: BOD ... an indicator of organic pollution
x: BOD is the key indicator of organic pollution in rivers and lakes. TDS and pH describe salts and acidity, not organic load.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.65

from_notes: Coliform count | Faecal contamination (MPN/100 ml)
x: A high coliform count indicates faecal contamination, i.e. contamination by human (and animal) wastes, not hydrocarbons or phosphorus.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.71; app notes 5:101 sub 1

from_notes: Coliform count | Faecal contamination
x: A higher coliform count is the indicator of mixing of human faeces. High BOD and low DO show organic pollution in general, not specifically faeces.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.71; app notes 5:101 sub 1
dispute: Official key / most books: higher total coliform. Strictly: faecal coliform / E. coli is the specific faecal indicator; total coliform also includes soil bacteria.

from_notes: Ganga is polluted by faecal coliform bacteria in its entire length.
x: Coliform bacteria from human faeces are the predominant pollutant of the Ganga; PMF notes the river is polluted by faecal coliform along its entire length.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.71

from_notes: Industrial Effluents: Discharge of organic wastes from industries pollutes water bodies.
x: Industrial and domestic effluents change the pH, DO, turbidity and chemistry of water sources. Macrophytes, fungi and evapotranspiration are natural, minor influences.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.10-11; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.64

from_notes: Various oxides of metals like copper, mercury, cadmium, chromium
x: Sulphur dioxide is a gaseous air pollutant (acid rain). Zinc, copper and nickel are heavy metals that contaminate water.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.11; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.66

from_notes: Suspended solids | Retained on a filter: silt, clay (APPSC 2023)
x: Silt is the standard example of a suspended solid (retained on a filter). Sodium is dissolved.
source: app notes 5:101 sub 1 (APPSC 2023); PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.64
dispute: Official key / most books: Silt. Strictly: faecal matter and fibres also occur as suspended solids in sewage; silt is the textbook example.

from_notes: Turbidity | Measured in NTU
x: NTU (nephelometric turbidity unit) measures turbidity, the cloudiness caused by suspended solids. It does not measure pressure, temperature or acidity.
source: app notes 5:101 sub 1; general knowledge, not checked

x: Water holds far less dissolved oxygen than air, so aquatic organisms must respire (ventilate) faster to get enough oxygen. Water is denser, not lighter, than air.
source: general knowledge, not checked (printed key agrees)

from_notes: Discharge of plant nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium into water bodies leads to the growth of oxygen-consuming algal populations
x: Eutrophication is the over-supply (enrichment) of nutrients such as nitrates and phosphates to a water body, causing algal blooms and loss of oxygen. It is not drying, flooding or a lack of nutrients.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.12; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.74

from_notes: Discharge of plant nutrients ... into water bodies leads to the growth of oxygen-consuming algal populations
x: During eutrophication excess nutrients enter the water. Algae then bloom (not get destroyed) and DO falls.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.12; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.74

from_notes: Discharge of plant nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium into water bodies
x: Eutrophication is an increased load of nutrients (N, P) in a water body; algal populations increase rather than decrease. Fluoride and lead are unrelated.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.12; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.74

from_notes: Discharge of plant nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium into water bodies
x: Eutrophication is an increased load of nutrients (N, P) in a water body; algal populations increase rather than decrease. Fluoride and lead are unrelated.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.12; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.74

from_notes: This process deoxygenates the water, resulting in the killing of aquatic organisms
x: Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment of a water body, and decomposition of the algal bloom depletes dissolved oxygen, so both statements are correct.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.12; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.73-74

from_notes: This process deoxygenates the water, resulting in the killing of aquatic organisms
x: Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment of a water body, and decomposition of the algal bloom depletes dissolved oxygen, so both statements are correct.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.12; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.73-74

from_notes: The presence of large amounts of nutrients in water results in an algal bloom ... which leads to the ageing of lakes.
x: Eutrophication is the natural ageing of a lake by nutrient enrichment, and nitrogen and phosphorus are the nutrients that drive it, so both statements are correct.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.73-74

from_notes: This process is known as natural eutrophication.
x: Eutrophication is the natural ageing of a lake by biological (nutrient) enrichment of its water. Toxicant build-up along trophic levels is biomagnification.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.73-74

from_notes: algal bloom ... which leads to the ageing of lakes
x: The natural ageing of a lake by nutrient enrichment is eutrophication. Biomagnification is the build-up of toxicants up the food chain.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.73-74

from_notes: Nitrate/phosphate | Eutrophication
x: Eutrophication results from high amounts of nitrogenous nutrients and phosphates entering the water body. Algal blooms and oxygen depletion are its effects, not its cause.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.12; Rocket Environment (src/environment/rocket-environment.txt) p.22

from_notes: The presence of large amounts of nutrients in water results in an algal bloom (excessive growth of planktonic algae)
x: Large amounts of nutrients cause excessive growth of planktonic algae (an algal bloom), which deteriorates water quality and kills fish, so both statements are correct.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.73

from_notes: Dead zones (biological deserts or hypoxic zones) are areas in the ocean with very low oxygen concentrations
x: Hypoxia is a reduction of oxygen in water (or air) that threatens aerobic organisms, as in dead zones formed after algal blooms. It is not an increase in oxygen.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.77

from_notes: Hypoxic zones can occur naturally (due to the upwelling of excess nutrients).
x: Nutrients from estuaries, monsoon run-off from land and upwelling of nutrient-rich deep water all feed harmful algal blooms, so all three are correct.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.77; app notes 5:101 sub 3

from_notes: Blooms of pigmented dinoflagellates in estuaries = red tides.
x: Blooms of pigmented dinoflagellates that colour estuarine and coastal water are called red tides.
source: app notes 5:101 sub 3; general knowledge, not checked

from_notes: The alteration of physical, chemical, and biological characteristics of water due to the presence of foreign materials results in water pollution.
x: Both statements are correct: water pollution is the release of harmful substances into water bodies, and it is controlled by wastewater treatment and regulation of industry and farming.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.9; PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.64

from_notes: Anthropogenic sources mainly include untreated or partially treated domestic sewage
x: Untreated domestic sewage is the largest source of water pollution in India; only about 28% of urban sewage is treated.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.64; app notes 5:101 sub 6

from_notes: Fertilizers containing nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium; pesticides
x: Chemical fertilisers and excessive chemical pesticides are the agricultural practices that mainly pollute water. Deforestation is not an agricultural practice, and livestock manure is a lesser source.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.11

from_notes: Sand mining | Raises turbidity, degrades river beds
x: Heavy sand mining pollutes groundwater and lowers the water table (UPSC 2018 key: B and C). It does not decrease river salinity; if anything saline intrusion rises.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.64; app notes 5:101 sub 0

from_notes: MBR (membrane bioreactor) | Activated sludge + membrane filtration
x: A membrane bioreactor combines activated-sludge treatment with membrane filtration and is a wastewater treatment technology, not a reproductive, drug-delivery or vaccine technology.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.84 (activated sludge); app notes 5:101 sub 6

from_notes: MBR (membrane bioreactor) | Activated sludge + membrane filtration
x: A membrane bioreactor combines activated-sludge treatment with membrane filtration and is a wastewater treatment technology.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.84 (activated sludge); app notes 5:101 sub 6

from_notes: the heavy floc particles to settle as sludge
x: Sludge is the settled solid by-product of sewage treatment; its anaerobic digestion yields biogas. Sewage is the raw input and scum floats.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.81, p.83

from_notes: Sewage: Improperly treated sewage can contaminate water sources.
x: Treating domestic sewage before release protects water bodies. Burning plastic or leaves pollutes air, and chemical fertilisers cause eutrophication.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.10

from_notes: Ozone gas may also be used to disinfect drinking water.
x: Ozone kills micro-organisms in water (it is used to disinfect drinking water), and ozone is indeed not radioactive, but that is not why it disinfects – it is a strong oxidant.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.81

x: Rain collected after 30–40 minutes of rain is largely free of dust and bacteria, but it is almost distilled water and deficient in minerals.
source: general knowledge, not checked (printed CDS key)

from_notes: India's first CETP: Andhra Pradesh (Jeedimetla, near Hyderabad), 1989
x: India's first Common Effluent Treatment Plant for small-scale industry clusters began at Jeedimetla near Hyderabad (then Andhra Pradesh) in 1989.
source: app notes 5:101 sub 6 (India's first CETP: Jeedimetla, 1989); general knowledge, not checked

x: In January 2023 researchers at IISER Pune reported a new porous material that captures toxic pollutants from water.
source: general knowledge, not checked (printed key agrees)

from_notes: In terms of arsenic and iron pollution, WB and Assam are the worst affected.
x: Arsenic contamination of groundwater is worst in West Bengal (with Assam), in the Ganga-Brahmaputra plains. Haryana, Rajasthan and MP are fluoride/salinity areas.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.67; Rocket Environment (src/environment/rocket-environment.txt) p.22

from_notes: Arsenic | Kolkata
x: Groundwater of the Bengal basin (West Bengal, Bangladesh) is mainly contaminated by arsenic. Rocket links arsenic with Kolkata.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.67; Rocket Environment (src/environment/rocket-environment.txt) p.22

from_notes: The non-biotic pollutant of underground water is ... Arsenic
x: Arsenic is a non-living (abiotic) chemical contaminant of groundwater; bacteria, algae and viruses are biotic agents.
source: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 (src/environment/nextgen-environment-appsc-10.txt) p.13

from_notes: Pollutants such as fluorides, uranium ...
x: Arsenic, fluoride and uranium occur as drinking-water pollutants in parts of India; sorbitol and formaldehyde do not, so 1, 3 and 5 is correct.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.67-68

from_notes: Pollutants such as fluorides, uranium ...
x: Arsenic, fluoride and uranium occur as drinking-water pollutants in parts of India; sorbitol and formaldehyde do not, so 1, 3 and 5 is correct.
source: PMF Environment Part 04 (src/environment/pmf-environment-04.txt) p.67-68

x: Nalgonda district is the best-known fluorosis-endemic area of Telangana, with high fluoride in groundwater (hence the 'Nalgonda technique' of defluoridation).
source: app notes 5:101 sub 5 (Nalgonda technique); general knowledge, not checked

x: The UP Ground Water (Management and Regulation) Act does penalise pollution of groundwater through boring pipes (fine and jail), so that statement is wrong. Registration of submersible pumps and rainwater harvesting in private schools/colleges are part of it.
